newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU says Belgium, UK breaking its TV rules.
newsitem.headline: EU says Belgium, UK breaking its TV rules.

text.p: The European Court of Justice ruled on Tuesday that Belgium and Britain are breaking European Union rules governing the way TV is broadcast across the 15-nation bloc.

The court said Belgium's French-speaking and Dutch-speaking regional governments had violated the EU's "TV without frontiers" directive by restricting programmes from other EU states that are carried on their cable networks.
It said Britain had broken the rules by claiming jurisdiction over broadcasters with a satellite uplink in Britain.
A central principle of the "TV without frontiers" directive is that national governments cannot bar broadcasts that comply with another EU state's laws.
Belgium's French- and Dutch-speaking governments were wrong to require cable distributors to seek prior authorisation to transmit programmes from other EU countries, the court said.

"A prior authorization or licensing system constitutes a serious obstacle to the free movement of broadcasts within the (EU) as provided for by the directive and has the effect of abolishing freedom to provide services," the court said in a statement.
In Britain's case, the court said the 1990 Broadcasting Act improperly gave the government control over non-domestic satellite broadcasts that were transmitted from Britain.

The European Commission had initiated the court case against Britain, saying broadcasters should be regulated in the EU state where they have their headquarters, not where they have a satellite uplink.
The ruling, however, is expected to have minimal impact in Britain, a spokeswoman for the British government said in Brussels.
"In practice, it affects only half a dozen broadcasters, none of the big ones," she said.

She said Britain was expecting to change its licensing regime anyway since EU states have provisionally agreed to revise the "TV without frontiers" directive where it applies to jurisdiction over broadcasters.
The revision would follow the thinking of the court, she said.
